## Prompting as a Conversation

Working with an AI tool doesn't have to be a single exchange — send a prompt, get a response, done. Most AI tools support back-and-forth conversations where each message can build on what came before.

When you use this effectively, follow-up prompts let you refine, redirect, or deepen the output without starting over. When you use it poorly, follow-ups can spiral into confusion, inconsistency, or a lot of wasted effort.

This page is about the difference.

## What a Good Follow-Up Does

A good follow-up does one of three things:

**1. Steers the output in a new direction.**
You got something useful, but you want to adjust a specific part — the tone, the structure, one argument, one function. A follow-up lets you make that adjustment without rewriting everything.

**2. Asks for clarification or deeper explanation.**
You got output you're not sure about. A follow-up asks the AI to explain its reasoning, walk you through a section, or justify a decision it made.

**3. Builds on what already exists.**
You got a solid first piece and you're ready to add the next part — another section, another function, a continuation.

## Reference Specific Parts of the Output

Vague follow-ups get vague results. The more specifically you reference what you're responding to, the more precise the response will be.

**Less effective:**
> *"Can you make this better?"*

The AI doesn't know what "better" means or which part you're talking about.

**More effective:**
> *"The second paragraph starts to get repetitive — can you tighten it so each sentence is making a distinct point?"*

> *"The conditional on line 8 — can you explain why you used `>=` there instead of `>`? I want to make sure I understand before I use this."*

> *"The CSS you gave me works on desktop, but the flex layout breaks at narrow widths. Can you add a media query that stacks the items vertically below 600px?"*

Specific references to the output make your follow-up more efficient and make the response more accurate.

## What Makes a Good Follow-Up vs. a Reset

Sometimes the right move is to continue the conversation. Sometimes it's to start fresh with a new prompt entirely. Knowing the difference saves time.

**Use a follow-up when:**
- The output was mostly right but needs a specific adjustment
- You want to build on something that's already working
- You're asking for explanation or reasoning about the output you received
- You're making a small correction or steering a particular section

**Start over (reset) when:**
- The output went in a fundamentally wrong direction and can't be steered back
- The context from earlier in the conversation is causing the AI to repeat the same mistake
- You've made so many follow-ups that the conversation is long and confused
- You've clarified your goal significantly and want a fresh start with that clarity built in from the beginning

When you reset, take what you learned from the previous attempt — especially the context and constraints that would have helped — and build them into the new prompt. The time spent on a failed attempt isn't wasted if you use it to write a better prompt.

## Avoid Prompt Spam

Prompt spam is sending multiple short, vague follow-ups in quick succession without giving the AI enough to work with.

It looks like this:
> *"Can you fix that?"*
> *"That's still not right."*
> *"Make it simpler."*
> *"Actually try again."*

Each of these follow-ups gives the AI little to go on. The result is usually a loop of outputs that are slightly different but still missing what you need.

Instead of sending vague corrections, pause and be specific:
- What exactly is wrong?
- What would "right" look like?
- What do you want it to do differently?

One specific follow-up beats five vague ones every time.

## Example: A Well-Used Follow-Up Sequence

**Prompt 1:**
> *"Write an opening paragraph for an essay arguing that school dress codes limit students' ability to express their identity. Audience is my English teacher. Aim for two to three sentences."*

**Output:** A paragraph that introduces the topic but reads more like a neutral overview than a clear argumentative stance.

**Follow-up 1:**
> *"This reads more like an introduction to a general topic than an argument. Can you revise it so it opens with a strong, direct claim instead of a broad observation?"*

**Output:** A paragraph that opens with a clear claim but uses vocabulary that feels too formal for the assignment.

**Follow-up 2:**
> *"Better — the claim is stronger now. Can you bring the language down slightly? It sounds more like a college essay than a high school one."*

**Output:** A paragraph that makes a clear argument in a natural voice.

That's three exchanges, each making one specific adjustment. No reset was needed because the direction was consistently moving toward what was needed.

## Example: Knowing When to Reset

You're working on a Python function that processes a list of temperatures and flags any outliers. You've gone back and forth five times and the function still has edge case issues.

At this point: look at what you now know that you didn't know at the start. You know that you need to handle empty lists, that "outlier" needs to be defined (you've decided to use more than 2 standard deviations from the mean), and that you want the function to return the flagged values, not just print them.

Write a new prompt with all of that built in from the start. That single clear prompt will likely get you further than a sixth follow-up on a tangled conversation.

## The Principle Behind It All

Follow-ups work best when you're steering, not hoping. Each one should have a clear purpose: adjust this, explain that, continue here.

Treat the conversation like a collaboration — you're directing, and you know where you're trying to go. The AI's job is to respond to what you give it. Your job is to give it something useful to respond to.
